6213.text: Find the positive value of '$a$' for which the equality $2\alpha + \beta = 8$ holds, where '$\alpha$' and '$\beta$' are the points of maximum and minimum, respectively, of the function $f ( x ) = 2x^{3} - 9ax^{2} + 12a^{2}x + 1$
6213.sol:
Given, $a > 0$

$f ( x ) = 2x^{3} - 9ax^{2} + 12a^{2}x + 1$

$f ' \left(x\right) = 6x^{2} - 18ax + 12a^{2}$

$f ' \left(x\right) = 6\left(x^{2} - 3ax + 2a^{2}\right)$

$f ' \left(x\right) = 6 \left(x - 2a\right)\left(x - a\right)$.

$x = a, x = 2a$

$f ' ' \left(x\right) = 6 \left(2x - 3a\right)$

$f ' ' \left(a\right) = 6\left(2a - 3a\right) <0$

$f ' ' \left(2a\right) =6\left(4a - 3a\right) >0$

Thus, \alpha = a, \beta = 2a$

$⇒ 2\alpha + \beta = 8$

$⇒ 2a + 2a = 8$

$⇒ 4a = 8$

$⇒ a = 2$

$

Assertion (A): $\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{(\sin x)^{\sqrt{2}} d x}{(\sin x)^{\sqrt{2}}+(\cos x)^{\sqrt{2}}}=\frac{\pi}{12}$
Reason (R): $\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \frac{f(x) d x}{f(x)+f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}=\frac{\pi}{12}$
options: A is true, $\mathrm{R}$ is true and $\mathrm{R}$ is the correct explanation of A
A is true, $\mathrm{R}$ is true but $\mathrm{R}$ is not the correct explanation of $\mathrm{A}$
9218.sol:
Let $\int_{\pi / 6}^{\pi / 3} \frac{(\sin x)^{\sqrt{2}} d x}{(\sin x)^{\sqrt{2}}+(\cos x)^{\sqrt{2}}}...(1)$
Since $\int_a^b f(x) d x=\int_a^b f(a+b-x) d x$
Hence $I=\int_{\pi / 6}^{\pi / 3} \frac{(\cos x)^{\sqrt{2}} \cdot d x}{(\sin x)^{\sqrt{2}}+(\cos x)^{\sqrt{2}}}...(2) \begin{aligned}& \text{ Equation (1)+(2), }\\
& \Rightarrow I \int_{1 / 3}^{/ 3} \frac{(\sin x)^{\sqrt{2}}(\cos x)^{\sqrt{2}}}{(\sin x)^{\sqrt{2}}(\cos x)^{\sqrt{2}}} d x \\
& \Rightarrow I=\frac{\pi}{12}

13380.text:

13380.sol:
$\begin{aligned} & \text{ (A) }[\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} \mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a} \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}] \\ & =(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) \times(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a}) \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \\ & =\{\mathbf{d} \times(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a})\} \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \\ & =\{(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{a}) \mathbf{c}-(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{c}) \mathbf{a}\} \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \\ & =\{[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}] \mathbf{c}-[\mathbf{b} \mathbf{c} \mathbf{c} \mathbf{\mathbf { a }}\} \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \\ & =\{[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{\mathbf { c }} \times \mathbf{c}-0\} \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \\ & =[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}]\{\mathbf{c} \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})\} \\ & =[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}][\mathbf{c} \mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}] \\ & =[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}]^2\end{aligned}$
(B)

$\begin{aligned}& {[\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{b}]} \\
& =\{(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \times(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c})\} \cdot \mathbf{b}\\
& =\{\mathbf{d} \times(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c})\} \cdot \mathbf{b} \quad[\text{ let } \mathbf{d}=\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}]\\
& =\{(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{c}) \mathbf{a}-(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{a}) \mathbf{c}\} \cdot \mathbf{b}\\
& =\{(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{c}\} \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}-\{(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{a}\} \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{b}\\
& =[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}][\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}]-[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{a}][\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{b}]\\
& =[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}][\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}]-0 \\
& =[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}][\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}]
\end{aligned}

($ C)

$$\begin{aligned}& {[\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b} \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c} \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}]} \\
& =(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}) \cdot\{(\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}) \times(\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a})\} \\
& =(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a})\\
& =(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a})[\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{c}=0] \\
& =\mathbf{a} \cdot(\mathbf{b} \times  \mathbf{c})+\mathbf{a}  \cdot( \mathbf{b}  \times  \mathbf{a})+\mathbf{a}  \cdot( \mathbf{c}  \times  \mathbf{a})\\
& +\mathbf{b} \cdot( \mathbf{b}  \times  \mathbf{c})+\mathbf{b}  \cdot( \mathbf{b}  \times  \mathbf{a})+\mathbf{b}  \cdot( \mathbf{c}  \times  \mathbf{a})\\
& =[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}]+0+0+0+0+[\mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}] \\
& =[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}]+[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}] \\
& =2[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}]
\end{aligned}$$

(D)  $\mathbf{a}$$, $$\mathbf{b}$$, $$\mathbf{c}$  are three mutually perpendicular units vector

$$\begin{aligned}& \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}=\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}=0 \\
& =[(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}) \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} \mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a}]\\
& =(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}) \cdot\{(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) \times(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a})\\
& =(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}) \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \quad[\because \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}=\mathbf{a} \text{ and } \mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a}=\mathbf{b}]\\
& =\mathbf{a} \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})+\mathbf{b} \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})+\mathbf{c} \cdot(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})\\
& =0+0+[\mathbf{c} \mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}] \\
& =[\mathbf{a} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}]
\end{aligned}$$

Hence, $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}$, $\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{IV}$, $\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{II}$, $\mathrm{D} \rightarrow$ III.$$

17236.text: A motor is used to deliver water at a certain rate through a given horizontal pipe. To deliver $n$-times the water through the same pipe in the same time the power of the motor must be increased as follows :
17236.sol:
If the motor pumps water (density $=\rho$ ) continuously through a pipe of area of crosssection $A$ with velocity $v$, then mass flowing out per second,
$m=A v \rho$ ...(i)
Rate of increase of kinetic energy
$=\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{2}(A v \rho) v^2$ ..(ii)
Mass $m$, flowing out per sec, can be increased to $m^{\prime}$ by increasing $v$ to $v^{\prime}$, then power increases from $P$ to $P^{\prime}$.
$\frac{P^{\prime}}{P}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} A \rho v^3}{\frac{1}{2} A \rho v^3}$
or $\quad \frac{P^{\prime}}{P}=\left(\frac{v^{\prime}}{v}\right)^3$
Now $\frac{m^{\prime}}{m}=\frac{A \rho v^{\prime}}{A \rho v}=\frac{v^{\prime}}{v}$
As $\quad m^{\prime}=n m, v^{\prime}=n v\therefore \quad \frac{P^{\prime}}{P}=n^3\Rightarrow \quad P^{\prime}=n^3 P$

20136.subject: Chemistry
20136.text: A current of 1.5 A is passed for 2 hours through an aqueous solution of $\mathrm{Pd} \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{n}}$ where X is a monovalent anion. During the electrolysis process 2.977 g of Palladium metal gets deposited at the cathode. Calculate the charge on Pd ions. (Atomic mass of Pd $=106.4 \mathrm{ g} / \mathrm{mol}$ ).
20136.sol:
The total charge $Q$ passed through the solution is given by $Q = I \times t$.

Given $I = 1.5$ A and $t = 2$ hours $= 2 \times 3600$ s $= 7200$ s.

$Q = 1.5 \times 7200 = 10800$ C.

The number of moles of electrons passed is $n_e = \dfrac{Q}{F} = \dfrac{10800}{96500} \approx 0.1119$ mol.

The mass of Palladium deposited is $m = 2.977$ g and the atomic mass is $M = 106.4$ g/mol.

The number of moles of Palladium deposited is $n_{Pd} = \dfrac{m}{M} = \dfrac{2.977}{106.4} \approx 0.02798$ mol.

The reaction at the cathode is $\mathrm{Pd}^{n+} + n e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Pd}$.

The stoichiometric ratio is $n = \dfrac{n_e}{n_{Pd}} = \dfrac{0.1119}{0.02798} \approx 4$.

Therefore, the charge on the Palladium ion is $n = 4$.

Answer: $\mathrm{n}=4$

20164.subject: Chemistry
20164.text: Propane in presence of $\mathrm{O}_2$ gas undergoes complete combustion to produce $\mathrm{CO}_2$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$. The required $\mathrm{O}_2$ for this combustion reaction was produced by the electrolysis of water. For what duration of time had water been electrolysed by passing $200 \mathrm{ A}$ current so that Oxygen gas produced could completely burn $44 \mathrm{ g}$ of Propane?
20164.sol:
The balanced chemical equation for the combustion of propane is:
$\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8} + 5\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_{2} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

The molar mass of propane ($\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8}$) is $3 \times 12 + 8 \times 1 = 44 \text{ g/mol}$.

Moles of propane = $\dfrac{44 \text{ g}}{44 \text{ g/mol}} = 1 \text{ mol}$.

From the stoichiometry, $1 \text{ mol}$ of propane requires $5 \text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_{2}$.

The electrolysis of water is given by:
$2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$

For $1 \text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_{2}$ produced, $4 \text{ moles}$ of electrons are required (since each oxygen atom changes oxidation state from $-2$ to $0$, and there are $2$ oxygen atoms per $\text{O}_{2}$ molecule).

Total moles of electrons required for $5 \text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_{2}$ = $5 \times 4 = 20 \text{ mol}$.

Using Faraday's law of electrolysis, $Q = n \times F = I \times t$, where $F \approx 96500 \text{ C/mol}$.

$20 \times 96500 = 200 \times t$

$t = \dfrac{20 \times 96500}{200} = 9650 \text{ seconds}$.

Converting to hours: $t = \dfrac{9650}{3600} \approx 2.68 \text{ hours}$.

Answer: 2.68 hours

20598.subject: Chemistry
20598.text: Which of the following show both Frenkel and Schottky defect?
20598.sol:
Frenkel defect arises due to the displacement of an ion from its lattice site to an interstitial site, typically occurring in ionic crystals where there is a large difference in size between the cation and the anion. Schottky defect arises due to the missing of equal numbers of cations and anions from the lattice sites to maintain electrical neutrality, typically occurring in ionic crystals with high coordination numbers and small differences in ionic sizes.

Silver bromide ($\mathrm{AgBr}$) is a unique case in solid state chemistry. Due to the intermediate size of the $\mathrm{Ag}^{+}$ ion, it is capable of showing both Frenkel defect (due to the small size of $\mathrm{Ag}^{+}$) and Schottky defect (due to the ionic nature and crystal structure).

$\mathrm{ZnS}$ primarily exhibits Frenkel defect. $\mathrm{NaCl}$ and $\mathrm{AgCl}$ primarily exhibit Schottky defect.

Answer: $\mathrm{AgBr}$

20637.subject: Chemistry
20637.text: An aqueous solution of volume V ml contains a non-volatile solute of unknown mass $W_B \mathrm{ g}$ and molar mass $M_B \mathrm{ g} / \mathrm{mol}$. If the Osmotic pressure of the solution is 1.013 bar , which one of the following is the mathematical expression to be used to calculate $W_B$ ?
20637.sol:
The osmotic pressure $\pi$ of a solution is given by the van't Hoff equation: $\pi = CRT$, where $C$ is the molar concentration of the solute in mol/L, $R$ is the universal gas constant, and $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin.

The molar concentration $C$ is defined as the number of moles of solute $n_B$ divided by the volume of the solution $V_L$ in liters. Given the mass of the solute $W_B$ in grams and its molar mass $M_B$ in g/mol, the number of moles is $n_B = \dfrac{W_B}{M_B}$.

The volume of the solution is given as $V$ ml. Converting this to liters, we have $V_L = \dfrac{V}{1000}$ L.

Substituting these into the expression for concentration: $C = \dfrac{n_B}{V_L} = \dfrac{W_B / M_B}{V / 1000} = \dfrac{W_B \times 1000}{M_B \times V}$.

Substituting $C$ back into the osmotic pressure equation: $\pi = \left( \dfrac{W_B \times 1000}{M_B \times V} \right) RT$.

Rearranging the equation to solve for $W_B$: $W_B = \dfrac{\pi M_B V}{1000 RT}$.

Answer: $W_B=\dfrac{\pi \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{B}} V}{1000 \mathrm{RT}}$

20679.subject: Chemistry
20679.text: The solution which have lowest freezing point is
20679.sol:
The freezing point depression is given by the formula $\Delta T_f = i \times K_f \times m$, where $i$ is the van't Hoff factor, $K_f$ is the cryoscopic constant, and $m$ is the molality. Since $K_f$ is constant for a given solvent and the molarity $M$ is given as $0.2 \mathrm{M}$ for all solutions, the freezing point depression is directly proportional to the van't Hoff factor $i$. The solution with the highest $i$ will have the lowest freezing point.

For $0.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$: $\mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{K}^{+} + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}$, so $i = 3$.

For $0.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{KCl}$: $\mathrm{KCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{K}^{+} + \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, so $i = 2$.

For $0.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaNO}_3$: $\mathrm{NaNO}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}^{+} + \mathrm{NO}_3^{-}$, so $i = 2$.

For $0.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{MgSO}_4$: $\mathrm{MgSO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+} + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}$, so $i = 2$.

Comparing the values of $i$, the solution with $i = 3$ will have the largest depression in freezing point, resulting in the lowest freezing point.

Answer: $0.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$

the mid-point of $P Q$. Find the distance of $L$ from the plane $3 x+4 z+25=0$
22216.sol:
Let coordinate of $D$ is $(x, y, z)$.
Using mid-point formula,

$\begin{aligned}Q &=\left(\frac{x-6}{2}, \frac{y-9}{2}, \frac{z+0}{2}\right)\\
\text{ Also, } \quadP &=\left(\frac{2+6}{2}, \frac{3+9}{2}, \frac{0+0}{2}\right)=(4,6,0)
\end{aligned}

Since, A C \| P Q \begin{aligned}&\therefore \text{ D.R'.s$ of $line }A C=\text{ D.R' s of line }P Q \\
&\Rightarrow(-8,-12,0)=\left(\frac{x-14}{2}, \frac{y-21}{2}, \frac{z}{2}\right)\\
&\Rightarrow x=-2, y=-3, z=0 \\
&\Rightarrow D(-2,-3,0) \Rightarrow Q(-4,-6,0)
\end{aligned}

If$ L$ is mid-point of $P Q$, then

L\left(\frac{4-4}{2}, \frac{6-6}{2},0\right)=(0,0,0)

$\therefore$ Perpendicular distance of $L(0,0,0)$ from the plane 3 x+4 z+25=0$ is

$\left|\frac{3(0)+4(0)+25}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}}}\right|=\left|\frac{25}{\sqrt{25}}\right|=\sqrt{25}=5
$

22630.text: A metal wire is subjected to a constant potential difference. When the temperature of the metal wire increases, the drift velocity of the electron in it
options: increases, thermal velocity of the electron decreases
decreases, thermal velocity of the electron decreases
increases, thermal velocity of the electron increases
decreases, thermal velocity of the electron increases
22630.sol:
Drift velocity of the electron is given as v_{d}=$\frac{e E \tau}{m}$ where, $e=$ charge on electron,
$E=$ electric field,
$\tau=$ relaxation time
and $m=$ mass of the electron.
Since, \therefore \quad v_{d}=$\frac{e V \tau}{m l}$ Since, $e, V, m$ and $l$ are constant . \therefore \quad v_{d} \propto \tau On increasing the temperature of metal wire, relaxation time decreases, therefore drift velocity of electrons also decreases.
But on increasing temperature of metal wire, thermal velocity of electron increases.

22816.subject: Physics
22816.text: Two identical conducting balls having unequal positive charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ are separated by a distance $r$. If they are made to touch each other and then separated to the same distance, the force between them will be
22816.sol:
Initial force: $F_1 = k\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$

After touching, each ball gets charge $q' = \dfrac{q_1+q_2}{2}$

New force: $F_2 = k\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{q_1+q_2}{2}\right)^2}{r^2}$

Comparing: since $q_1 \neq q_2$, $(q_1-q_2)^2 > 0$

$\Rightarrow (q_1+q_2)^2 > 4q_1q_2 \Rightarrow \left(\dfrac{q_1+q_2}{2}\right)^2 > q_1q_2$

$\therefore F_2 > F_1$, the force is more than before.

23775.subject: Physics
23775.text: When water falls from a height of $80 \mathrm{ m}$ at the rate of $20 \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$ to operate a turbine the losses due to frictional force are $20 \%$ of input energy. How much power is generated by the turbine?
23775.sol:
The potential energy of the water falling per unit time is the input power, given by $P_{in} = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = \left(\dfrac{m}{t}\right)gh$.

Given $\dfrac{m}{t} = 20 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$, $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, and $h = 80 \text{ m}$, we have $P_{in} = 20 \times 10 \times 80 = 16000 \text{ W} = 16 \text{ kW}$.

The losses due to frictional force are $20 \%$ of the input energy, so the efficiency of the turbine is $100 \% - 20 \% = 80 \%$.

The power generated by the turbine is $P_{out} = 80 \% \text{ of } P_{in} = 0.8 \times 16 \text{ kW} = 12.8 \text{ kW}$.

Answer: 12.8 KW

25931.subject: Mathematics
25931.text:
Consider the following lists:

List-$I$ List-$II$
$\left(I\right)$ $\left\{x \in \left[- \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right]: cosx + sinx = 1\right\}$ $\left(P\right)$ has two elements
$\left(II\right)$ $\left\{x \in \left[- \dfrac{5\pi}{18}, \dfrac{5\pi}{18}\right]: \sqrt{3}tan3x = 1\right\}$ $\left(Q\right)$ has three elements
$\left(III\right)$ $\left\{x \in \left[- \dfrac{6\pi}{5}, \dfrac{6\pi}{5}\right]: 2cos\left(2x\right) = \sqrt{3}\right\}$ $\left(R\right)$ has four elements
$\left(IV\right)$ $\left\{x \in \left[- \dfrac{7\pi}{4}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right]: sinx - cosx = 1\right\}$ $\left(S\right)$ has five elements
$\left(T\right)$ has six elements

The correct option is:
25931.sol:
Solving all questions one by one we get,

(i) $\left\{x \in \left[\dfrac{- 2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right], cosx + sinx = 1\right\}$

$cosx + sinx = 1$

$⇒ sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + x\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\pi}{4} + x = n\pi + {\left(- 1\right)}^{n}\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

$⇒ x = n\pi + {\left(- 1\right)}^{n}\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

So, $x \in \left\{0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}$

$∴ x$ has $2$ elements.$\to P$

(ii) $\left\{x \in \left[\dfrac{- 5\pi}{18}, \dfrac{5\pi}{18}\right]: \sqrt{3}tan3x = 1\right\}$

Solving $\sqrt{3}tan3x = 1$

$⇒ tan3x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$⇒ 3x = n\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{n\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{18}$

So, $x \in \left\{\dfrac{\pi}{18}, \dfrac{- 5\pi}{18}\right\}$

$∴ x$ has $2$ elements. $\to P$

(iii) $\left\{x \in \left[\dfrac{- 6\pi}{5}, \dfrac{6\pi}{5}\right]: 2cos2x = \sqrt{3}\right\}$

$2cos2x = \sqrt{3}$

$⇒ cos2x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$⇒ 2x = 2n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

$⇒ x = n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{12}$

So, $x \in \left\{\pm \dfrac{\pi}{12}, \pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{12}, - \pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{12}\right\}$

$∴ x$ has $6$ elements.$\to T$

(iv) $\left\{x \in \left[\dfrac{- 7\pi}{4}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right]: sinx - cosx = 1\right\}$

$sinx - cosx = 1$

$⇒ sin\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ x - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = n\pi + {\left(- 1\right)}^{n}\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

$⇒ x = n\pi + {\left(- 1\right)}^{n}\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

So, $x \in \left\{\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{- 3\pi}{2}, \pi, - \pi\right\}$

$∴ x$ has $4$ elements. $\to R$

$∴$ option $B$ is correct.

Consider the following species:

Number of species having sp$^3$d hybridized central atom is __________.
27700.sol:
The steric number $H$ is calculated as $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(V + M - C + A)$, where $V$ is the number of valence electrons on the central atom, $M$ is the number of monovalent atoms, $C$ is the cationic charge, and $A$ is the anionic charge.

For $sp^3d$ hybridization, $H = 5$.

BrF$_5$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(7 + 5) = 6$ ($sp^3d^2$)

XeF$_5^-$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(8 + 5 + 1) = 7$ ($sp^3d^3$)

BF$_4^-$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(3 + 4 + 1) = 4$ ($sp^3$)

ICl$_4^-$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(7 + 4 + 1) = 6$ ($sp^3d^2$)

XeF$_4$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(8 + 4) = 6$ ($sp^3d^2$)

SF$_4$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(6 + 4) = 5$ ($sp^3d$)

NH$_4^+$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(5 + 4 - 1) = 4$ ($sp^3$)

ClF$_3$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(7 + 3) = 5$ ($sp^3d$)

XeF$_2$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(8 + 2) = 5$ ($sp^3d$)

ICl$_2^-$: $H = \dfrac{1}{2}(7 + 2 + 1) = 5$ ($sp^3d$)

The species with $sp^3d$ hybridization are SF$_4$, ClF$_3$, XeF$_2$, and ICl$_2^-$.

The number of such species is $4$.

Answer: $4$

30407.subject: Chemistry
30407.text: One mole of an alkane (x) requires $8$ mole oxygen for complete combustion. Sum of number of carbon and hydrogen atoms in the alkane (x) is _______.
30407.sol:
The general formula of an alkane is $C_n H_{2n+2}$.

The balanced chemical equation for the complete combustion of an alkane is:

$C_n H_{2n+2} + \left(\dfrac{3n+1}{2}\right) O_2 \rightarrow n CO_2 + (n+1) H_2O$

Given that $1$ mole of the alkane requires $8$ moles of oxygen for complete combustion, we equate the stoichiometric coefficient of $O_2$ to $8$:

$\dfrac{3n+1}{2} = 8$

$3n + 1 = 16$

$3n = 15$

$n = 5$

The molecular formula of the alkane is $C_5H_{12}$.

The number of carbon atoms is $5$ and the number of hydrogen atoms is $12$.

Sum of the number of carbon and hydrogen atoms $= 5 + 12 = 17$.

Answer: $17$

31589.text: Consider the bcc unit cells of the solids $1$ and $2$ with the position of atoms as shown below. The radius of atom $B$ is twice that of atom $A .$ The unit cell edge length is $50%$ more in solid $2$ than in $1$ . What is the approximate packing efficiency in solid $2$ ?
31589.sol:
If radius of $A$ is $r$ radius of $B$ will be $2r$ . Atoms in the body diagonal touch.

Therefore:
$r + 2r + 2r + r = \sqrt{3}a$

$6r = \sqrt{3}a$ or $a = \dfrac{6r}{\sqrt{3}}$

Packing Efficiency
$= \dfrac{1 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{r}^{3} + 1 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{( 2r )}^{3}}{{a}^{3}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi{r}^{3} \times 9}{{( 6r / \sqrt{3} )}^{3}}$
$= \dfrac{4 \times 9 \times \pi \times {r}^{3} \times 3\sqrt{3}}{3 \times 216 \times {r}^{3}} = 90.5%$

32925.text: The shortest distance between the line $x - y = 1$ and the curve ${x}^{2} = 2y$ is:
32925.sol:
Shortest distance between curves is always along common normal.

Let $P\left({x}_{0}, {y}_{0}\right)$ be any point on the parabola ${x}^{2} = 2y$.

Clearly, slope of line $x - y = 1$ is $1$.

Hence, slope of perpendicular line is $- 1$.

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}P =$Slope of tangent at $P$

Therefore, $\dfrac{- 1}{\dfrac{dy}{dx}P} =$Slope of normal$= - 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx}P = 1$

$⇒ {x}_{0} = 1 ∴ {y}_{0} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ P\left(1, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

$∴$ Shortest distance $= \left|\dfrac{1 - \dfrac{1}{2} - 1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2} + {1}^{2}}}\right| = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$

option $\left(3\right)$

35189.text: Suppose $f: R \to \left(0, \infty\right)$ be a differentiable function such that $5f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) \cdot f\left(y\right), ∀ x, y \in R$, If $f\left(3\right) = 320$, then $\mathop{∑}_{n = 0}^{5}f\left(n\right)$ is equal to:
35189.sol:
Given, equation is:

$5f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) \cdot f\left(y\right) . . . \left(1\right)$

At $x = 0, y = 0$, we get

$5f\left(0\right) = f{\left(0\right)}^{2} ⇒ f\left(0\right) = 5$

Put $y = 1$ in $\left(1\right)$, then we get

$5f\left(x + 1\right) = f\left(x\right) \cdot f\left(1\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{f\left(x + 1\right)}{f\left(x\right)} = \dfrac{f\left(1\right)}{5}$

$⇒ \dfrac{f\left(1\right)}{f\left(0\right)} \cdot \dfrac{f\left(2\right)}{f\left(1\right)} \cdot \dfrac{f\left(3\right)}{f\left(2\right)} = {\left(\dfrac{f\left(1\right)}{5}\right)}^{3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{320}{5} = \dfrac{{\left(f\left(1\right)\right)}^{3}}{{5}^{3}} ⇒ f\left(1\right) = 20$

$∴ 5f\left(x + 1\right) = 20 \cdot f\left(x\right)$

$⇒ f\left(x + 1\right) = 4f\left(x\right)$

So,

$f\left(1\right) = 4f\left(0\right) = 4 \cdot 5f\left(2\right) = 4f\left(1\right) = {4}^{2} \cdot 5f\left(3\right) = 4f\left(2\right) = {4}^{3} \cdot 5f\left(4\right) = 4f\left(3\right) = {4}^{4} \cdot 5f\left(5\right) = 4f\left(4\right) = {4}^{5} \cdot 5$

$\mathop{∑}_{n = 0}^{5}f\left(n\right) = 5 + 5 \cdot 4 + 5 \cdot {4}^{2} + 5 \cdot {4}^{3} + 5 \cdot {4}^{4} + 5 \cdot {4}^{5}$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{n = 0}^{5}f\left(n\right) = \dfrac{5\left({4}^{6} - 1\right)}{3} = 6825$

35257.sol:
$fof ( x ) = \dfrac{a - f\left(x\right)}{a + f ( x )} = x$

$⇒ \dfrac{a - ax}{1 + x} = f ( x )$

$⇒ \dfrac{a ( 1 - x )}{1 + x} = \dfrac{a - x}{a + x}$ $( ∵ a = 1 )$

so $f ( x ) = \dfrac{1 - x}{1 + x}$

$f\left(- \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 3$

36813.text: Consider the quadratic equation $(n^2 - 2n + 2)x^2 - 3x + (n^2 - 2n + 2)^2 = 0$, $n \in \mathbb{R}$. Let $\alpha$ be the minimum value of the product of its roots and $\beta$ be the maximum value of the sum of its roots. Then the sum of the first six terms of the G.P., whose first term is $\alpha$ and the common ratio is $\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}$, is :
36813.sol:
The given quadratic equation is $(n^2 - 2n + 2)x^2 - 3x + (n^2 - 2n + 2)^2 = 0$.

Let $k = n^2 - 2n + 2 = (n-1)^2 + 1$. Since $(n-1)^2 \ge 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{R}$, the minimum value of $k$ is $1$ at $n=1$.

The product of the roots is given by $P = \dfrac{(n^2 - 2n + 2)^2}{n^2 - 2n + 2} = n^2 - 2n + 2 = k$.

The minimum value of the product of the roots is $\alpha = \min(k) = 1$.

The sum of the roots is given by $S = \dfrac{3}{n^2 - 2n + 2} = \dfrac{3}{k}$.

The maximum value of the sum of the roots occurs when $k$ is minimum. Thus, $\beta = \max\left(\dfrac{3}{k}\right) = \dfrac{3}{1} = 3$.

We are given a Geometric Progression (G.P.) whose first term is $a = \alpha = 1$ and common ratio is $r = \dfrac{\alpha}{\beta} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

The sum of the first six terms of this G.P. is:

$S_6 = a \dfrac{1 - r^6}{1 - r} = 1 \cdot \dfrac{1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^6}{1 - \dfrac{1}{3}}$

$S_6 = \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{1}{729}}{\dfrac{2}{3}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{728}{729}}{\dfrac{2}{3}}$

$S_6 = \dfrac{728}{729} \times \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{364}{243}$

Answer: $\dfrac{364}{243}$

36820.text: If the quadratic equation $(\lambda+2)x^2-3\lambda x+4\lambda=0$, $\lambda \neq -2$, has two positive roots, then the number of possible integral values of $\lambda$ is:
36820.sol:
For the quadratic equation $(\lambda+2)x^2-3\lambda x+4\lambda=0$ to have two positive roots, the following three conditions must be satisfied:

1. Discriminant $D \ge 0$
$(-3\lambda)^2 - 4(\lambda+2)(4\lambda) \ge 0$
$9\lambda^2 - 16\lambda^2 - 32\lambda \ge 0$
$-7\lambda^2 - 32\lambda \ge 0$
$7\lambda^2 + 32\lambda \le 0$
$\lambda(7\lambda + 32) \le 0$
$\lambda \in \left[-\dfrac{32}{7}, 0\right]$

2. Sum of roots $> 0$
$\alpha + \beta = \dfrac{3\lambda}{\lambda+2} > 0$
$\lambda \in (-\infty, -2) \cup (0, \infty)$

3. Product of roots $> 0$
$\alpha \beta = \dfrac{4\lambda}{\lambda+2} > 0$
$\lambda \in (-\infty, -2) \cup (0, \infty)$

Taking the intersection of all three conditions, we get:
$\lambda \in \left[-\dfrac{32}{7}, -2\right)$

Since $-\dfrac{32}{7} \approx -4.57$, the possible integral values of $\lambda$ in this interval are $-4$ and $-3$.

Thus, there are $2$ possible integral values of $\lambda$.

Answer: $2$

36868.sol:
Given,

${e}^{8x} - {e}^{6x} - 3{e}^{4x} - {e}^{2x} + 1 = 0$

$⇒ {e}^{4x} - {e}^{2x} - 3 - \dfrac{1}{{e}^{2x}} + \dfrac{1}{{e}^{4x}} = 0$

$⇒ {e}^{4x} + \dfrac{1}{{e}^{4x}} + 2 - \left({e}^{2x} + \dfrac{1}{{e}^{2x}}\right) = 5$

$⇒ {\left({e}^{2x} + \dfrac{1}{{e}^{2x}}\right)}^{2} - \left({e}^{2x} + \dfrac{1}{{e}^{2x}}\right) = 3$

Now let $\left({e}^{2x} + \dfrac{1}{{e}^{2x}}\right) = t$

So, the equation becomes

${t}^{2} - t - 5 = 0$

$⇒ t = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{21}}{2}$, ignoring negative sign as exponential function are positive,

Now ${e}^{2x} + \dfrac{1}{{e}^{2x}} = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{21}}{2}$

$⇒ {e}^{4x} - \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{21}}{2}{e}^{2x} + 1 = 0$ which is quadratic equation in ${e}^{2x}$ with upward parabola,

Now by $A . M \ge G . M$ we get, ${e}^{2x} + \dfrac{1}{{e}^{2x}} \ge 2$

So, $y = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{21}}{2} > 2$, hence it will cut at two distinct point,

Hence, there will be two solution.

37012.text: Let $\alpha = 3+4+8+9+13+14+\ldots$ upto 40 terms. If $(\tan\beta)^{\frac{\alpha}{1020}}$ is a root of the equation $x^2+x-2=0$, $\beta \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, then $\sin^2\beta + 3\cos^2\beta$ is equal to:
37012.sol:
The given series is $\alpha = 3+4+8+9+13+14+\ldots$ up to $40$ terms.

We can split the series into two arithmetic progressions, each containing $20$ terms:

$S_1 = 3 + 8 + 13 + \ldots$ up to $20$ terms

$S_2 = 4 + 9 + 14 + \ldots$ up to $20$ terms

Using the sum formula for an AP, $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n-1)d]$:

$S_1 = \dfrac{20}{2}[2(3) + (20-1)5] = 10[6 + 95] = 1010$

$S_2 = \dfrac{20}{2}[2(4) + (20-1)5] = 10[8 + 95] = 1030$

Therefore, $\alpha = S_1 + S_2 = 1010 + 1030 = 2040$.

The exponent in the given expression is $\dfrac{\alpha}{1020} = \dfrac{2040}{1020} = 2$.

Thus, $(\tan\beta)^2 = \tan^2\beta$ is a root of the equation $x^2+x-2=0$.

Solving $x^2+x-2=0$ gives $(x+2)(x-1)=0 \Rightarrow x = -2$ or $x = 1$.

Since $\tan^2\beta \ge 0$, we must have $\tan^2\beta = 1$.

Given $\beta \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\tan\beta = 1 \Rightarrow \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

We need to find the value of $\sin^2\beta + 3\cos^2\beta$.

Substituting $\beta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

$\sin^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + 3\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 + 3\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{3}{2} = 2$.

Answer: $2$

37966.text:
Let the line of the shortest distance between the lines ${L}_{1}: \overset{\to}{r} = \left(\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right)$ + \lambda $\left(\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}\right)$ and ${L}_{2}: \overset{\to}{r} =\left(4\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j} + 6\overset{^}{k}\right) + \mu \left(\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right) intersect${L}_{1} and {L}_{2}$ at $P and Q$ respectively. If \left(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\right) is the midpoint of the line segment $PQ$, then $2$\left(\alpha + \beta + \gamma\right) is equal to___________

$
37966.sol:
Let point on ${L}_{1}$ be $P\left(\left(1 + \lambda\right)\overset{^}{i} + \left(2 - \lambda\right)\overset{^}{j} + \left(3 + \lambda\right)\overset{^}{k}\right)$ and point on ${L}_{2}$ be $Q\left(\left(4 + \mu\right)\overset{^}{i} + \left(5 + \mu\right)\overset{^}{j} + \left(6 - \mu\right)\overset{^}{k}\right)$.

$⇒ \overset{\to}{PQ} = \left(\lambda - \mu - 3\right)\overset{^}{i} + \left(- \lambda - \mu - 3\right)\overset{^}{j} + \left(\lambda + \mu - 3\right)\overset{^}{k}$

Now, $\overset{\to}{PQ} ⊥ {L}_{1}, {L}_{2}$

$⇒ \left(\lambda - \mu - 3\right) + \left(\lambda + \mu + 3\right) + \left(\lambda + \mu - 3\right) = 0$

$⇒ 3\lambda + \mu = 3 . . . \left(i\right)$

Also, $\left(\lambda - \mu - 3\right) + \left(- \lambda - \mu - 3\right) + \left(- \lambda - \mu + 3\right) = 0$

$⇒ - \lambda - 3\mu = 3 . . . \left(ii\right)$

Now, solving above equations we get,

$⇒ 3\lambda + \mu - 3\lambda - 9\mu = 3 + 9$

$⇒ - 8\mu = 12$

$⇒ \mu = \dfrac{- 3}{2}$

$⇒ \lambda = \dfrac{3}{2}$

$⇒ P ≡ \left(\dfrac{5}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{9}{2}\right), Q ≡ \left(\dfrac{5}{2}, \dfrac{7}{2}, \dfrac{15}{2}\right)$

So, mid-point of $PQ$ is $\left(\dfrac{5}{2}, 2, 6\right)$

$⇒ 2\left(\alpha + \beta + \gamma\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{5}{2} + 2 + 6\right)$

$⇒ 2\left(\alpha + \beta + \gamma\right) = 21$

38395.text: If $tan15 ° + \dfrac{1}{tan75 °} + \dfrac{1}{tan105 °} + tan195 ° = 2a$, then the value of $\left(a + \dfrac{1}{a}\right)$ is :
38395.sol:
Given:

$2a = tan15 ° + \dfrac{1}{tan75 °} + \dfrac{1}{tan105 °} + tan195 °$

$⇒ 2a = tan15 ° + \dfrac{1}{tan\left(90 ° - 15 °\right)} + \dfrac{1}{tan\left(90 ° + 15 °\right)} + tan\left(180 ° + 15 °\right)$

$⇒ 2a = tan15 ° + \dfrac{1}{cot15 °} - \dfrac{1}{cot15 °} + tan15 °$

$⇒ 2a = 2tan15 °$

$⇒ a = tan15 °$

$⇒ a = tan\left(45 ° - 30 °\right)$

$⇒ a = \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}$

$⇒ a = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{\sqrt{3} + 1}$

So,

$a + \dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{\sqrt{3} + 1} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{\sqrt{3} - 1}$

$⇒ a + \dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{{\left(\sqrt{3} - 1\right)}^{2} + {\left(\sqrt{3} + 1\right)}^{2}}{2}$

$⇒ a + \dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4$

38786.text: The primary side of a transformer is connected to $230V, 50Hz$ supply. The turn ratio of primary to secondary winding is $10: 1$. Load resistance connected to the secondary side is $46Ω$. The power consumed in it is:
38786.sol:
The voltages associated with the primary and the secondary side of the transformer are related to the turn ratio as follows:

$\dfrac{{V}_{1}}{{V}_{2}} = \dfrac{{N}_{1}}{{N}_{2}} . . . \left(1\right)$

From equation (1), it follows that

$\dfrac{230}{{V}_{2}} = \dfrac{10}{1}$

${V}_{2} = 23V$

Hence, the power consumed can be calculated as follows

$\begin{cases}P & = & {V}_{2}^{2}R \\ & = & \dfrac{23 \times 23}{46} \\ & = & 11 . 5W\end{cases}$

Let velocity before collision v from momentum conservation $mv = ( m + m ){v}^{1}$

${v}^{1} = \dfrac{v}{2}$

Loss in K.E. $= \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2m\right){\left(\dfrac{v}{2}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{1}{4}m{v}^{2}$

K.E. lost is used to jump from ${1}^{st}$ orbit to ${2}^{nd}$ orbit $∆ K . E . = 10.2eV$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{4}m{v}^{2} = 10.2$

$\dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = 2 \times 10.2 = 20.4eV$

40305.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Electromagnetic waves carry energy as they travel through space and this energy is equally shared by the electric and magnetic fields.

Statement II: When electromagnetic waves strike a surface, a pressure is exerted on the surface.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
40305.sol:
Electromagnetic wave carries energy shared equally in magnetic and electric field which is given by, $= \dfrac{1}{2}{ε}_{0}{E}^{2} = \dfrac{{B}^{2}}{2{\mu}_{0}}$, as $E = cB$ and ${c}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{{\mu}_{0}{ε}_{0}}$.

Also, Electromagnetic wave carries momentum and therefore exerts force when it strikes a surface.

41530.text:
Two long parallel conductors ${S}_{1}$ and ${S}_{2}$ are separated by a distance $10cm$ and carrying currents of $4A$ and $2A$ respectively. The conductors are placed along $x$-axis in $X - Y$ plane. There is a point $P$ located between the conductors (as shown in figure).
A charge particle of $3\pi$ coulomb is passing through the point $P$ with velocity $\overset{\to}{v} = \left(2\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j}\right)m{s}^{- 1}$; where $\overset{^}{i}$ & $\overset{^}{j}$ represents unit vector along $x$ & $y$axis respectively.
The force acting on the charge particle is $4\pi \times {10}^{- 5}\left(- x\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j}\right)N$. The value of $x$ is
41530.sol:
Net magnetic field at $P$ is ${B}_{Net} = \left(\dfrac{{\mu}_{0} \times {i}_{1}}{2\pi{r}_{1}} - \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}{i}_{2}}{2\pi{r}_{2}}\right)\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$

${B}_{Net} = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}4}{2\pi \times \dfrac{4}{100}} - \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}2}{2\pi \times \dfrac{6}{100}}$

$= \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}}{\pi} \times 100\left[\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{6}\right]$

$= \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}}{\pi} \times 100\left[\dfrac{4}{2 \times 6}\right]$

$= \dfrac{{\mu}_{0} \times 100}{3\pi}\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$

So, force acting on charge particle is$\overset{\to}{F} = q\left(\overset{\to}{v} \times \overset{\to}{B}\right) = 3\pi\left[2\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j}\right]\dfrac{{\mu}_{0} \times 100}{3\pi}\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$

$= 4\pi \times {10}^{- 7}\left[2\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j}\right] \times 100\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$

$= 4\pi \times {10}^{- 5}\left[2\overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{i}\right]$

$∴ x = 3$

44416.text: The ratio of speed of sound in hydrogen gas to the speed of sound in oxygen gas at the same temperature is:
44416.sol:
The formula to calculate the speed of sound in hydrogen gas is given by

${v}_{{H}_{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gammaRT}{{M}_{{H}_{2}}}} . . . \left(1\right)$

The formula to calculate the speed of sound in oxygen is given by

${v}_{{O}_{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gammaRT}{{M}_{{O}_{2}}}} . . . \left(2\right)$

Divide equation (1) by (2) and simplify to obtain the required ratio.

$\dfrac{{v}_{{H}_{2}}}{{v}_{{O}_{2}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{M}_{{O}_{2}}}{{M}_{{H}_{2}}}} . . . \left(3\right)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (3) to calculate the required ratio.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{{v}_{{H}_{2}}}{{v}_{{O}_{2}}} & = & \sqrt{\dfrac{32}{2}} \\ & = & 4: 1\end{cases}$

54847.subject: Chemistry
54847.text: Which among the following has highest melting point ?
54847.sol:
p-Nitrophenol has the highest melting point among the given compounds.

In p-nitrophenol, there is strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the -OH group of one molecule and the -N$O_2$ group of another molecule. This leads to the association of molecules, requiring more thermal energy to break the crystal lattice.

In contrast, o-nitrophenol exhibits intramolecular hydrogen bonding (chelation), which restricts molecular association and lowers its melting point.

Phenol and p-cresol also exhibit intermolecular hydrogen bonding, but the interactions are weaker compared to p-nitrophenol. Additionally, the highly symmetrical structure of p-nitrophenol allows it to pack more efficiently in the solid state, further increasing its melting point.

Answer: p-Nitrophenol

55138.subject: Chemistry
55138.text:
Identify the products of following reaction?
$\text{ Formaldehyde }+ \text{ Benzaldehyde } \xrightarrow[\text{ ii) } \mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{O}^{+}]{\text{i) conc. } \mathrm{NaOH}} $$\text{ Products }$
55138.sol:
Crossed Cannizzaro Reaction of Formaldehyde and Benzaldehyde

Formaldehyde ($\mathrm{HCHO}$) and benzaldehyde ($\mathrm{C_6 H_5CHO}$) are both aldehydes lacking alpha-hydrogens, qualifying them for the Cannizzaro reaction. In crossed Cannizzaro reactions, formaldehyde is preferentially oxidized due to its greater reactivity, while the partner aldehyde is reduced.

Concentrated $\mathrm{NaOH}$ initiates hydride transfer: formaldehyde is oxidized to formate ion ($\mathrm{HCOO^-}$), which upon acidification yields methanoic acid ($\mathrm{HCOOH}$). Benzaldehyde is reduced to benzyl alkoxide ($\mathrm{C_6 H_5CH_2 O-}$), producing phenylmethanol ($\mathrm{C_6 H_5CH_2 OH}$) after acid workup.

$\mathrm{HCHO}$ oxidizes to $\mathrm{HCOOH}$, while $\mathrm{C_6 H_5CHO}$ reduces to $\mathrm{C_6 H_5CH_2 OH}$.

The products are methanoic acid and phenylmethanol, corresponding to option C.

Counting the carbon atoms:
Two $-\text{CH}_2-$ groups $\rightarrow 2$ carbon atoms

Two $-\text{CH}_3$ groups $\rightarrow 2$ carbon atoms

57561.subject: Chemistry
57561.text: Identify the product 'B' in the following reaction sequence.
57561.sol:
The given reaction sequence involves the formation of a Grignard reagent followed by its reaction with an alcohol.

Step 1: The reactant 2-chlorobutane reacts with magnesium (Mg) in the presence of dry ether to form a Grignard reagent, sec-butylmagnesium chloride (A).
$CH_3-CH_2-CH(Cl)-CH_3 \xrightarrow{\text{Mg, Dry ether}} CH_3-CH_2-CH(MgCl)-CH_3$

Step 2: Grignard reagents are strong bases and react vigorously with compounds containing acidic hydrogen atoms, such as alcohols, water, and amines, to form alkanes. Ethanol ($C_2H_5OH$) provides an acidic proton.
The sec-butylmagnesium chloride abstracts a proton from ethanol to form butane (B) and an alkoxide salt.
$CH_3-CH_2-CH(MgCl)-CH_3 + C_2H_5OH \rightarrow CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3 + Mg(OC_2H_5)Cl$

Therefore, the final product 'B' is butane, which corresponds to the skeletal structure shown in the second option.

57592.subject: Chemistry
57592.text: Which of the following reagents is used in the preparation of nitroalkane from haloalkane?
57592.sol:
Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution with nitrite ions ($\text{NO}_2^-$), which are ambident nucleophiles capable of attacking through either oxygen or nitrogen atoms.

Alkali metal nitrites like KNO_2$ and NaNO_2$ are predominantly ionic, with oxygen's higher electronegativity making it the preferred nucleophilic site, yielding alkyl nitrites: R–X + KNO_2$\rightarrow R–O–N=O + KX.

Silver nitrite (AgNO_2$) is covalent, with the Ag–O bond reducing oxygen's nucleophilicity and favoring nitrogen attack, producing nitroalkanes: R–X + AgNO_2$\rightarrow R–NO_2$ + AgX.

To prepare nitroalkanes from haloalkanes, silver nitrite is the preferred reagent.

57759.subject: Chemistry
57759.text: Identify the catalyst used in the Friedel crafts acylation reaction.
57759.sol:
Friedel-Crafts acylation is an electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction in which an acyl group is introduced into an aromatic ring.

The reaction requires a strong Lewis acid catalyst to facilitate the generation of the electrophilic acylium ion from an acyl halide or acid anhydride.

Anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ is the standard and most widely used Lewis acid catalyst for this purpose.

The general reaction is:
$\text{ArH} + \text{RCOCl} \xrightarrow{\text{Anhydrous AlCl}_3} \text{ArCOR} + \text{HCl}$

Answer: Anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$

58841.text: What is the total number of different types of unit cells in tetragonal crystal system?
58841.sol:
The tetragonal crystal system is defined by unit cell parameters where $a = b \neq c$ and $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90^{{}^{\circ}}$.

Two Bravais lattice types exist in this system:

A primitive (P) tetragonal unit cell contains lattice points only at the corners.

A body-centered (I) tetragonal unit cell has points at the corners and one at the body center.

This gives a total of two distinct unit cells in the tetragonal system.

The correct answer is B.

58845.subject: Chemistry
58845.text: What is the the coordination number of a particle in simple cubic close packed structure?
58845.sol:
The coordination number in a crystal lattice is defined as the number of nearest neighbors to a particle.

In a simple cubic structure, each atom is positioned at the corners of a cube. A central atom contacts six adjacent atoms: one each along the positive and negative directions of the $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes.

Thus, the coordination number is $6$.

Although simple cubic is not a close-packed structure like FCC or HCP (which have coordination number $12$), the result remains consistent.

Final answer: $\boxed{C}$

60214.sol:
Let $y = \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^x = x^{-x}$

Taking natural logarithm on both sides:

$\ln y = -x \ln x$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{1}{y} \dfrac{dy}{dx} = - \left( \ln x + x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} \right) = -(\ln x + 1)$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -x^{-x}(\ln x + 1)$

For maximum or minimum value, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$

$-x^{-x}(\ln x + 1) = 0$

Since $x^{-x} \neq 0$ for $x > 0$, we have $\ln x + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{1}{e}$

For $0 < x < \dfrac{1}{e}$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} > 0$ and for $x > \dfrac{1}{e}$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} < 0$

Thus, $y$ attains its maximum value at $x = \dfrac{1}{e}$

The maximum value is $y_\max = \left(\dfrac{1}{1/e}\right)^{1/e} = e^{1/e}$

Answer: $e^{1/e}$

62548.text: If $y = \tan^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{\sqrt{1 + x^2} - \sqrt{1 - x^2}}{\sqrt{1 + x^2} + \sqrt{1 - x^2}}\right\}$, where $|x| < 1$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is equal to
62548.sol:
Let $x^2 = \cos 2\theta$. Then $\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(x^2)$.

Substituting this into the given expression, we get:

$\sqrt{1 + x^2} = \sqrt{1 + \cos 2\theta} = \sqrt{2\cos^2\theta} = \sqrt{2}\cos\theta$

$\sqrt{1 - x^2} = \sqrt{1 - \cos 2\theta} = \sqrt{2\sin^2\theta} = \sqrt{2}\sin\theta$

Now, substitute these into $y$:

$y = \tan^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\cos\theta - \sqrt{2}\sin\theta}{\sqrt{2}\cos\theta + \sqrt{2}\sin\theta}\right\}$

Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $\sqrt{2}\cos\theta$:

$y = \tan^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{1 - \tan\theta}{1 + \tan\theta}\right\}$

$y = \tan^{-1}\left\{\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \theta\right)\right\}$

$y = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \theta$

Substituting back $\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(x^2)$:

$y = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(x^2)$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{1 - (x^2)^2}}\right) \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2)$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}} \cdot 2x$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}}$

63636.text: Three urns respectively contain 2 white and 3 black, 3 white and 2 black and 1 white and 4 black balls. If one ball is drawn from each urn, then the probability that the selection contains 1 black and 2 white balls is
63636.sol:
Solution:

Let each urn contain 5 balls. The probability of drawing white from urn 1 is $P(W_1)=\frac{2}{5}$, black $P(B_1)=\frac{3}{5}$.
For urn 2: $P(W_2)=\frac{3}{5}$, $P(B_2)=\frac{2}{5}$.
For urn 3: $P(W_3)=\frac{1}{5}$, $P(B_3)=\frac{4}{5}$.

The selection of one black and two white balls occurs in three mutually exclusive cases:
Black from urn 1: $\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{1}{5}=\frac{9}{125}$
Black from urn 2: $\frac{2}{5}\times\frac{2}{5}\times\frac{1}{5}=\frac{4}{125}$
Black from urn 3: $\frac{2}{5}\times\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{4}{5}=\frac{24}{125}$

The total probability sums to $\frac{9}{125}+\frac{4}{125}+\frac{24}{125}=\frac{37}{125}$.

$\boxed{\frac{37}{125}}$

64358.text: The angle between the line $\bar{r} = (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}) + \lambda(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})$ and the plane $\bar{r} \cdot (2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = 8$ is $\ldots$
64358.sol:
The direction vector of the given line is $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

The normal vector to the given plane is $\vec{n} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

The angle $\theta$ between a line and a plane is given by the formula:

$\sin \theta = \dfrac{|\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n}|}{|\vec{b}| |\vec{n}|}$

Calculating the dot product:

$\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n} = (1)(2) + (1)(-1) + (1)(1) = 2 - 1 + 1 = 2$

Calculating the magnitudes of the vectors:

$|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{3}$

$|\vec{n}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{6}$

Substituting these values into the formula:

$\sin \theta = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3} \sqrt{6}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{18}} = \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$

$\theta = \sin^{-1} \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)

Answer: $\theta = \sin^{-1}$\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)$

64404.subject: Mathematics
64404.text: The point of intersection of the two lines $\dfrac{x-3}{3} = \dfrac{y-3}{-1}, z - 1 = 0$ and $\dfrac{x-6}{2} = \dfrac{z-1}{3}, y - 2 = 0$ is....
64404.sol:
The equations of the first line can be written as $\dfrac{x-3}{3} = \dfrac{y-3}{-1} = t$ and $z = 1$.

Any point on the first line is of the form $(3t+3, -t+3, 1)$.

The equations of the second line can be written as $\dfrac{x-6}{2} = \dfrac{z-1}{3} = s$ and $y = 2$.

Any point on the second line is of the form $(2s+6, 2, 3s+1)$.

At the point of intersection, the coordinates must be equal.

Equating the $y$-coordinates, we get $-t+3 = 2 \Rightarrow t = 1$.

Equating the $z$-coordinates, we get $1 = 3s+1 \Rightarrow s = 0$.

Substituting $t = 1$ in the coordinates of the first line, we get the point $(6, 2, 1)$.

Substituting $s = 0$ in the coordinates of the second line, we also get the point $(6, 2, 1)$.

Thus, the point of intersection is $(6, 2, 1)$.

Answer: $(6, 2, 1)$

65095.text: The volume of a parallelopiped with coterminous edges $\bar{a}, \bar{b}, \bar{c}$ is 3 cubic units. The volume (in cubic units) of a tetrahedron with coterminous edges $(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}), (\bar{a} \times 2\bar{c}), (\bar{b} \times 2\bar{c})$ is...
65095.sol:
The volume of the parallelopiped with coterminous edges $\bar{a}, \bar{b}, \bar{c}$ is given by $|[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]| = 3$.

The volume of a tetrahedron with coterminous edges $\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z}$ is $V = \dfrac{1}{6} |[\bar{x} \bar{y} \bar{z}]|$.

Here, the edges are $\bar{x} = \bar{a} \times \bar{b}$, $\bar{y} = 2(\bar{a} \times \bar{c})$, and $\bar{z} = 2(\bar{b} \times \bar{c})$.

Evaluating the scalar triple product of these edges:

$[\bar{x} \bar{y} \bar{z}] = [\bar{a} \times \bar{b} \quad 2(\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) \quad 2(\bar{b} \times \bar{c})] = 4 [\bar{a} \times \bar{b} \quad \bar{a} \times \bar{c} \quad \bar{b} \times \bar{c}]$

Using the scalar triple product expansion:

$[\bar{a} \times \bar{b} \quad \bar{a} \times \bar{c} \quad \bar{b} \times \bar{c}] = (\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \cdot ((\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) \times (\bar{b} \times \bar{c}))$

Applying the vector triple product formula:

$(\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) \times (\bar{b} \times \bar{c}) = [\bar{a} \bar{c} \bar{c}] \bar{b} - [\bar{a} \bar{c} \bar{b}] \bar{c}$

Since $[\bar{a} \bar{c} \bar{c}] = 0$ and $[\bar{a} \bar{c} \bar{b}] = -[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]$, we get:

$(\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) \times (\bar{b} \times \bar{c}) = [\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}] \bar{c}$

Substituting this back into the scalar triple product:

$(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \cdot ([\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}] \bar{c}) = [\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}] ((\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \cdot \bar{c}) = [\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]^2$

Therefore, the scalar triple product of the new edges is:

$[\bar{x} \bar{y} \bar{z}] = 4 [\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]^2$

Since $|[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]| = 3$, we have $[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]^2 = 9$.

$[\bar{x} \bar{y} \bar{z}] = 4 \times 9 = 36$

The volume of the tetrahedron is $V = \dfrac{1}{6} \times 36 = 6$ cubic units.

Answer: $6$

65105.text: Let $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$. If $\vec{c}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} = |\vec{c}|$, $|\vec{c} - \vec{a}| = 2\sqrt{2}$ and the angle between $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ is $60^{}^{\circ}$, then $|(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}|$ is equal to
65105.sol:
Given $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

The magnitude of $\vec{a}$ is $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2 + (-2)^2} = 3$.

Squaring the given equation $|\vec{c} - \vec{a}| = 2\sqrt{2}$ yields:

$|\vec{c}|^2 + |\vec{a}|^2 - 2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} = 8$

Substituting $|\vec{a}| = 3$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} = |\vec{c}|$:

$|\vec{c}|^2 + 9 - 2|\vec{c}| = 8$

$|\vec{c}|^2 - 2|\vec{c}| + 1 = 0$

$(|\vec{c}| - 1)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow |\vec{c}| = 1$

Calculating the cross product $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$:

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}) \times (\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = -3\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$

The magnitude is $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (-3)^2} = 3\sqrt{2}$.

The angle between $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ is $60^{}^{\circ}$.

Using the definition of the cross product magnitude:

$|(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}| = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| |\vec{c}| \sin 60^{}^{\circ}$

$|(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}| = (3\sqrt{2})(1)\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{3\sqrt{6}}{2} = 3\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$

Answer: $3\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$

66070.sol:
The relationship between charge and voltage for a capacitor is given by $Q = CV$, which rearranges to $V = \frac{1}{C}Q$.

Comparing this with the standard linear form $y = mx$, the slope of the V-Q graph equals $\frac{1}{C}$.

Since capacitor B's graph has a steeper slope than A's, we have $\frac{1}{C_B} > \frac{1}{C_A}$, and thus $C_B < C_A$.

Therefore, capacitor B has smaller capacitance than capacitor A.

Final answer: $\boxed{B}$

70445.text: A Pipe open at one end has length $0.8$ m. At the open end of the tube a string $0.5$ m long is vibrating in its first overtone and resonates with fundamental frequency of pipe. If tension in the string is $50$ N, the mass of string is (Neglect end correction) (Speed of sound $= 320$ m/s)
70445.sol:
The fundamental frequency of a pipe open at one end (closed pipe) is given by $f_p = \dfrac{v}{4L_p}$.

Substituting the given values, $f_p = \dfrac{320}{4 \times 0.8} = 100$ Hz.

The string is vibrating in its first overtone, which corresponds to the second harmonic. The frequency of the string is $f_s = \dfrac{2}{2L_s} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \dfrac{1}{L_s} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$.

Since the string resonates with the pipe, $f_s = f_p$.

$\dfrac{1}{0.5} \sqrt{\dfrac{50}{\mu}} = 100$

$2 \sqrt{\dfrac{50}{\mu}} = 100 \Rightarrow \sqrt{\dfrac{50}{\mu}} = 50$

Squaring both sides, we get $\dfrac{50}{\mu} = 2500 \Rightarrow \mu = \dfrac{50}{2500} = 0.02$ kg/m.

The mass of the string is $m = \mu L_s = 0.02 \times 0.5 = 0.01$ kg.

Converting to grams, $m = 10$ g.

Answer: $10$ gram

71035.subject: Biology
71035.text:
Which of the following are functional units of an ecosystem?
A. Productivity.
B. Spatial pattern.
C. Nutrient cycling.
D. Energy flow.
E. Decomposition.
options: A, B, C and D only
A, C, D and E only
A, B, C and E only
71035.sol:
The components of an ecosystem are seen to function as a unit when the following aspects are considered:
1. Productivity
2. Decomposition
3. Energy flow
4. Nutrient cycling

Spatial pattern (such as stratification) is a structural feature of an ecosystem, not a functional unit.

Therefore, the functional units are Productivity (A), Nutrient cycling (C), Energy flow (D), and Decomposition (E).

Answer: A, C, D and E only

Swarts reaction is the best method for the preparation of alkyl fluorides. In this reaction, alkyl chlorides or bromides are heated in the presence of metallic fluorides such as $AgF$, $Hg_2F_2$, $CoF_2$, or $SbF_3$ to form alkyl fluorides.

$R-X + AgF \rightarrow R-F + AgX$ (where $X = Cl, Br$)

Finkelstein reaction is used for the preparation of alkyl iodides.

Sandmeyer's reaction is used for the preparation of aryl halides.

Wurtz reaction is used for the preparation of higher alkanes.

Answer: Swartz reaction

71879.subject: Chemistry
71879.text: The solubility product of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ is $4 \times 10^{-12}$. What is the amount of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ in gram present in $100$ ml its saturated solution? (molar mass of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4 = 331.73$ g/mol).
71879.sol:
Let the solubility of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ be $s$ mol/L.

The dissociation reaction is:
$\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}^+ + \text{CrO}_4^{2-}$

The solubility product $K_{sp}$ is given by:
$K_{sp} = [\text{Ag}^+]^2 [\text{CrO}_4^{2-}] = (2s)^2(s) = 4s^3$

Given $K_{sp} = 4 \times 10^{-12}$, we have:
$4s^3 = 4 \times 10^{-12}$
$s^3 = 10^{-12}$
$s = 10^{-4}$ mol/L

The number of moles of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ in $100$ ml (0.1$ L) of saturated solution is:
Moles $= s \times V = 10^{-4} \times 0.1 = 10^{-5}$ mol

The amount of \text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ in grams is:
Mass $= \text{Moles} \times \text{Molar mass}$
Mass $= 10^{-5} \times 331.73 = 3.3173 \times 10^{-3}$ g

Answer: $3.3173 \times 10^{-3}$ g

72140.subject: Physics
72140.text: An unknown resistance wire in the left gap of a meter bridge balances a $10\ \Omega$ resistance in the right gap at a point that divides the bridge wire in a ratio $3:2$. If the length of this unknown resistance wire is $1.5\ \text{m}$, what is its resistance per unit length? (Bridge wire is uniform)
72140.sol:
Let the unknown resistance in the left gap be $R$ and the resistance in the right gap be $S = 10\ \Omega$.

At the balance point of the meter bridge, the ratio of resistances is equal to the ratio of the lengths of the bridge wire segments:

$\dfrac{R}{S} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2}$

Given that the balance point divides the bridge wire in the ratio $3:2$, we have:

$\dfrac{R}{10} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

$R = 10 \times \dfrac{3}{2} = 15\ \Omega$

The length of the unknown resistance wire is $L = 1.5\ \text{m}$.

The resistance per unit length of the wire is:

$\dfrac{R}{L} = \dfrac{15}{1.5} = 10.0\ \Omega/\text{m}$

Answer: $10.0\ \Omega/\text{m}$

72262.subject: Physics
72262.text: The magnetic field inside the solenoid is
options: inversely proportional to total number of turns
72262.sol:
The magnetic field inside a long solenoid is given by the formula:

$B = \mu_0 n I$

where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length ($n = \dfrac{N}{L}$) and $I$ is the current flowing through the solenoid.

From the formula, it is clear that the magnetic field $B$ is directly proportional to the current $I$ ($B \propto I$).

It is directly proportional to the total number of turns $N$ and inversely proportional to the length $L$.

Thus, the magnetic field is directly proportional to the current.

Answer: directly proportional to current

72384.subject: Physics
72384.text: The depletion region of a p-n junction is formed due to
options: drift of majority carriers under the influence of an applied electric field.
thermal energy exciting electrons from the p-side to the n-side.
diffusion of majority carriers across the junction immediately after formation, leaving behind fixed immobile ions.
the physical removal of material at the junction interface during manufacturing
72384.sol:
When a p-n junction is formed, there is a concentration gradient of charge carriers across the junction.

Due to this gradient, majority carriers diffuse across the junction. Holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side, and electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side.

As these mobile charge carriers cross the junction, they leave behind uncompensated, fixed immobile ions (negative acceptor ions on the p-side and positive donor ions on the n-side).

This region near the junction, which is depleted of mobile charge carriers and contains only fixed immobile ions, is called the depletion region.

Answer: diffusion of majority carriers across the junction immediately after formation, leaving behind fixed immobile ions.

77540.text:
Consider the following in respect of inverse circular functions :
I. $\sin^{-1}(-x)=-\sin^{-1}x$
II. $\cos^{-1}(-x)=\cos^{-1}x$
III. $\tan^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\tan^{-1}x$
IV. $\cot^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cot^{-1}x$
How many of the above are correct ?
77540.sol:
Statement I: $\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1}x$ is a standard property of inverse trigonometric functions and is correct.

Statement II: The correct property is $\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x$. Hence, this statement is incorrect.

Statement III: The correct property is $\tan^{-1}(-x) = -\tan^{-1}x$. Hence, this statement is incorrect.

Statement IV: $\cot^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cot^{-1}x$ is a standard property and is correct.

Exactly two of the given statements are correct.

80821.subject: Chemistry
80821.text:
Match the species in List I with their geometry in List II
List IList II
A. PCl$_5$I. Tetrahedral
B. BrF$_5$II. Square Planar
C. BF$_4^-$III. Trigonal bipyramidal
D. [Ni(CN)$_4$]$^{2-}$IV. Square pyramidal
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
80821.sol:
For $\text{PCl}_5$, the central atom $\text{P}$ has $5$ valence electrons. It forms $5$ bond pairs with $\text{Cl}$ atoms and has $0$ lone pairs. The hybridization is $sp^3d$, and the geometry is trigonal bipyramidal. (A $\rightarrow$ III)

For $\text{BrF}_5$, the central atom $\text{Br}$ has $7$ valence electrons. It forms $5$ bond pairs with $\text{F}$ atoms and has $1$ lone pair. The hybridization is $sp^3d^2$, and the geometry is square pyramidal. (B $\rightarrow$ IV)

For $\text{BF}_4^-$, the central atom $\text{B}$ has $3$ valence electrons plus $1$ from the negative charge, giving $4$ electrons. It forms $4$ bond pairs with $\text{F}$ atoms and has $0$ lone pairs. The hybridization is $sp^3$, and the geometry is tetrahedral. (C $\rightarrow$ I)

For $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$, the central metal ion $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ has a $3d^8$ electronic configuration. Since $\text{CN}^-$ is a strong field ligand, it causes the pairing of electrons in the $3d$ orbitals. The hybridization is $dsp^2$, and the geometry is square planar. (D $\rightarrow$ II)

The correct matching is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

Answer: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

The formula to calculate the Newtonian force on the body is given by

$F = m{a}_{max} . . . \left(1\right)$

And, the frictional force on the body by the surface of the car is given by

$f = {\mu}_{s}mg . . . \left(2\right)$

Equate equations (1) and (2) and simplify to obtain the required maximum acceleration of the car.

$\begin{cases}m{a}_{max} & = & {\mu}_{s}mg \\ & ⇒ & {a}_{max} = {\mu}_{s}g . . . \left(3\right)\end{cases}$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (3) to calculate the required parameter.

$\begin{cases}{a}_{max} & = & 0 . 15 \times 10m{s}^{- 2} \\ = & 1 . 5m{s}^{- 2}\end{cases}$

84118.subject: Zoology
84118.text: Given below is the ECG of a normal human. Which one of its components is human, which one of its components is correctly interpreted below.
options: complex $Q R S-$ One complete pulse
peak T-Initiation of total cardiac contraction
peak $P$ and peak $R$ together-systolic and diastolic blood pressures
peak $P$-Initiation of left atrial contraction only
84118.sol:
A) The QRS complex represents the electrical impulse as it spreads through the ventricles and indicates ventricular depolarization. The QRS complex starts just before ventricular contraction and is the complete pulse.
B) The T wave represents the repolarization of the ventricles. Cardiac relaxation takes place.
C) The P wave represents the depolarization of the atria This happens right before the atria contract and push blood into the ventricles. R represents the peak of the ventricular contraction. Systole corresponds to contraction while diastole corresponds to relaxation. The P and R peaks only signify a systole.
D) T wave signifies the relaxation of the whole heart (diastole).
So the correct answer is 'QRS complex - one complete pulse'.

84921.text: In sea urchin DNA, which is double-stranded, $17 %$ of the bases were shown to be cytosine. What are the percentages of other three bases expected to be present in this DNA?
84921.sol:
In the DNA molecule, the nucleotides are base paired according to the Chargaff's rule of base equivalence, and it tells always tells adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine.

$A = T, G = C$

C = $17 %$So G = $17 %$

$A + G / T + C = 1$

$A + G + C + T = 100$

A + $17 + 17$+ T = $100$

A + T = $100 - 34$

So, $A = 33 % , T = 33 % = 66$

Reciprocals of $2, \dfrac{log ⁡ 4}{log ⁡ \left({3}^{x} - 4\right)}, \dfrac{log ⁡ 4}{log ⁡ \left({3}^{x} + \dfrac{7}{2}\right)}$ are in A.P.

91965.text: In ten observations, the mean of all $10$ numbers is $15$, the mean of the first six observations is $16$ and the mean of the last five observations is $12$. The sixth number is
91965.sol:
Let the mean of the last four observations be ${A}_{2}$. Then, by the formula for combined mean, we get,

$15 = \dfrac{6 \times 16 + 4 \times {A}_{2}}{6 + 4}$

or $150 = 96 + 4{A}_{2}$

$∴ {A}_{2} = \dfrac{54}{4}$

Let the sixth number is $x$, then taking the sixth number as a collection, the combined mean of this collection and the collection of the last four is $12$.

$∴$ By the definition of combined mean

$12 = \dfrac{1 \times x + 4 \times \dfrac{54}{4}}{1 + 4}$

$∴ 60 = x + 54 ∴ x = 6$

Hence, the sixth number $= 6$

Let,~$lo{g}_{2}cos\theta =t$

$⇒ t^{2} + $\left(\dfrac{4 + t}{2 - t}\right)$ =$2$
$⇒ 2t^{2} - t^{3} + 4 + t = 4 - 2t ⇒ t^{3} - 2t^{2} - 3t = 0$
$⇒ t = 0,3, - 1$ .
$t = 0 ⇒ lo{g}_{2}cos\theta =0 ⇒ cos\theta =1 ⇒ \theta =0$

$t = 3 ⇒ lo{g}_{2}cos\theta =3 ⇒ cos\theta =8$~(not possible)
$⇒$ Number of solutions are~$3$

$∴ \dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = \omega = 6 - 6{t}^{2}$

As, $\omega = 0$ (given)

$6 - 6{t}^{2} = 0$

${t}^{2} = \pm 1$

As, $t = - 1\text{s}$ is not possible, hence $t = 1\text{s} .$

Substituting $t = 1\text{s}$ in Equation (i), we get

${\theta}_{1} = 6 - 2 = 4\text{r}\text{a}\text{d}$

and ${\theta}_{0} = 6 \times 0 - 2 \times {0}^{2}\left(t = 0\right) = 0$

$∴$ Mean value of $\omega = \dfrac{{\theta}_{1} - {\theta}_{0}}{{t}_{1} - {t}_{0}} = \dfrac{4 - 0}{1 - 0} = 4\text{r}\text{a}\text{d}{\text{s}}^{- 1}$

93982.subject: Physics
93982.text: Which, among the following, is a correct statement?
options: binding energy of a nucleus is always negative
binding energy of a nucleus may be positive
higher value of binding energy per nucleon means the nucleus is more ununstable
higher value of binding energy per nucleon means the nucleus is more stable
93982.sol:
It has been observed that total mass of nucleus is always less than the sum of the masses of its nucleons. The energy difference between the nucleus and its constituent particles due to their mass difference is termed as the binding energy of the nucleus.
In other words, we can say that to break the nucleus into its constituent particles, some energy is needed to be supplied. This energy is termed as binding energy of the nucleus. More is the binding energy per nucleon, more is the energy required to break the nucleus and hence we can say the more stable the nucleus is.

100554.text: A particle is projected at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ from the horizontal with a speed of $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ on the earth. It's time of flight, range, velocity of impact are respectively $\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{R}, \mathrm{V}$. If this projectile is projected on the moon then its time of flight, range and velocity of impact is (assume gravitational field on moon is $\mathrm{g} / 6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
100554.sol:
Given, angle of projection, $\theta=30^{\circ}$ Initial speed of particle, $\mathrm{v}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
Time of flights, range and velocity of impact on the surface of earth are T, R and V respectively
$\therefore \quad \mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \mathrm{v} \sin \theta}{\mathrm{g}}, \mathrm{R}=\frac{\mathrm{v}^2 \sin 2 \theta}{\mathrm{g}}$
Gravitational acceleration on moon's surface is equal to $\frac{1}{6}$ part of gravitational acceleration on the earth's surface.
Hence,
$\begin{aligned}
& g_m=\frac{g_e}{6} \\
& T_m=\frac{2 v \sin \theta}{\frac{g}{6}}=\frac{6 \times 2 v \sin \theta}{g}=6 \mathrm{~T} \\
& R_m=\frac{v^2 \sin 2 \theta}{\frac{g}{6}}=\frac{6 v^2 \sin 2 \theta}{g}=6 R
\end{aligned}$
Velocity of impact will be same at both places of moon and earth.
$\therefore \quad \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{V}$

Match List I with List II :

  List I   List II
A Isothermal Process I Work done by the gas decreases internal energy
B Adiabatic Process II No change in internal energy
C Isochoric Process III The heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly to do work

102028.sol:
(A) Change in internal energy is expressed as$∆ U = n{C}_{v} ∆ T$, here, $∆ T$ is change in temperature.

Since, in an isothermal process temperature remains constant, thus, $∆ U = 0$

$A \to II$

(B) In an adiabatic process, heat transfer, $Q = 0$.

So, from first law of thermodynamics, 

$Q = ∆ U + W$

$∆ U = - W$

Since, work done by gas is positive, thus, $∆ U$ is negative

$B \to I$

(C) In an isochoric process, volume remains constant, so work done by or on the gas $W = P ∆ V = 0$

$C \to IV$

(D) In an isobaric process, pressure remains constant, so work done$W = P ∆ V \ne 0$ and change in internal energy $∆ U = n{C}_{v} ∆ T \ne 0$

Thus, heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly do work.

$D \to III$

103348.subject: Physics
103348.text: Five resistors are connected between four points A, C, D, and B arranged in a straight line in that order. The resistors are connected as follows: $3 \Omega$ between A and C, $15 \Omega$ between C and D, and $12 \Omega$ between D and B. Additionally, a $6 \Omega$ resistor connects A and D, and a $6 \Omega$ resistor connects C and B. A battery of unknown EMF $\varepsilon$ and a series resistor of $2 \Omega$ are connected across the terminals A and B. If the total current drawn from the battery is $1.5 \text{ A}$, what is the EMF of the battery?
103348.sol:
The given circuit can be redrawn to identify its standard topology. The nodes are A, C, D, and B.

The resistors are:
$R_{AC} = 3 \Omega$
$R_{CB} = 6 \Omega$
$R_{AD} = 6 \Omega$
$R_{DB} = 12 \Omega$
$R_{CD} = 15 \Omega$

This forms a Wheatstone bridge between terminals A and B, with C and D as the middle nodes. Let us check the balance condition:
$\dfrac{R_{AC}}{R_{CB}} = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$\dfrac{R_{AD}}{R_{DB}} = \dfrac{6}{12} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Since the ratios are equal, the bridge is balanced. No current flows through the central $15 \Omega$ resistor between C and D, so it can be removed from the calculation.

The equivalent resistance of the bridge $R_{bridge}$ is the parallel combination of the upper branch (A-C-B) and the lower branch (A-D-B):
$R_{upper} = 3 + 6 = 9 \Omega$
$R_{lower} = 6 + 12 = 18 \Omega$
$R_{bridge} = \dfrac{9 \times 18}{9 + 18} = \dfrac{162}{27} = 6 \Omega$

The total resistance of the circuit includes the series resistor:
$R_{total} = R_{bridge} + 2 = 6 + 2 = 8 \Omega$

Using Ohm's law, the EMF of the battery is:
$\varepsilon = I \times R_{total} = 1.5 \times 8 = 12.0 \text{ V}$

Answer: $12.0 \text{ V}$

103536.subject: Physics
103536.text: A thin straight bar magnet of magnetic moment $M$ is bent into an arc of a circle. If the new magnetic moment of the bent magnet is $\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}M}{\pi}$, the angle subtended by the arc at the centre of the circle is
103536.sol:
Let the initial length of the magnet be $L$ and its pole strength be $m$. The initial magnetic moment is $M = m \times L$.

When bent into an arc of a circle of radius $R$ subtending an angle $\theta$ (in radians) at the centre, the arc length is $L = R\theta \Rightarrow R = \dfrac{L}{\theta}$.

The new effective magnetic length $L^{\prime}$ is the straight-line distance (chord) between the poles:

$L^{\prime} = 2R \sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2L}{\theta} \sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$

The new magnetic moment is $M^{\prime} = m \times L^{\prime} = m \times \dfrac{2L}{\theta} \sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = M \left( \dfrac{2}{\theta} \sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) \right)$.

Given that $M^{\prime} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}M}{\pi}$, we have:

$\dfrac{2}{\theta} \sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\pi}$

$\dfrac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\theta} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\pi}$

By checking standard angles, if $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ ($90^{\circ}$):

$\dfrac{\sin(\pi/4)}{\pi/2} = \dfrac{1/\sqrt{2}}{\pi/2} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}\pi} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\pi}$.

Thus, the angle subtended at the centre is $90^{\circ}$.

Answer: $90^{\circ}$

103918.subject: Physics
103918.text: A metallic rod of length $1.0 \mathrm{~m}$ is pivoted at one end and rotated at a constant angular velocity of $20 \mathrm{~rad/s}$ in a uniform magnetic field of $0.5 \mathrm{~T}$ directed perpendicular to the plane of rotation. The free end of the rod slides on a circular conducting ring. If a resistor of $5 \Omega$ is connected between the pivot and the ring, what is the electrical power dissipated in the resistor?
103918.sol:
First, calculate the induced electromotive force (emf) across the ends of the rotating rod. The formula for the induced emf $\varepsilon$ is:
$\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2} B \omega L^2$

Given values:
$B = 0.5 \mathrm{~T}$
$\omega = 20 \mathrm{~rad/s}$
$L = 1.0 \mathrm{~m}$

Substituting the values:
$\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 20 \times (1.0)^2$
$\varepsilon = 0.5 \times 10 \times 1 = 5 \mathrm{~V}$

Next, calculate the electrical power $P$ dissipated in the resistor using the formula:
$P = \dfrac{\varepsilon^2}{R}$

Given $R = 5 \Omega$:
$P = \dfrac{(5)^2}{5} = \dfrac{25}{5} = 5 \mathrm{~W}$

If the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ factor in the emf formula is omitted, the emf would be calculated as $10 \mathrm{~V}$, leading to an incorrect power of $20 \mathrm{~W}$. If the formula $P = \varepsilon \times R$ is mistakenly used, the result would be $25 \mathrm{~W}$.

Answer: $5 \mathrm{~W}$

104996.text: An electron and a positron, both essentially at rest, undergo complete annihilation. If the rest mass energy of an electron is $0.511 \text{ MeV}$, the total energy released in this process is:
104996.sol:
In pair annihilation, an electron and a positron are completely converted into energy.

The mass of a positron is exactly equal to the mass of an electron.

Total mass converted into energy = $m_{e} + m_{e} = 2m_{e}$.

Given the rest mass energy of an electron is $0.511 \text{ MeV}$, the total energy released is:
$E = 2 \times 0.511 \text{ MeV} = 1.022 \text{ MeV}$.

The option with Joules is incorrect because the numerical value corresponds to the energy in MeV, not Joules.

Answer: $1.022 \text{ MeV}$

105270.text:
Consider a digital logic circuit with two inputs $A$ and $B$, and an output $Y$. The timing diagrams for the inputs and output show the following logic levels across four consecutive time intervals:

Input $A$: $0, 1, 0, 1$
Input $B$: $0, 0, 1, 1$
Output $Y$: $1, 0, 0, 0$

Which of the following logic circuit configurations produces this output?
options: Inputs $A$ and $B$ are fed directly into an AND gate.
Inputs $A$ and $B$ are fed directly into an OR gate.
Input $A$ is fed to a NOT gate, input $B$ is fed to a NOT gate, and their outputs are fed into an OR gate.
Input $A$ is fed to a NOT gate, input $B$ is fed to a NOT gate, and their outputs are fed into an AND gate.
105270.sol:
From the given logic levels across the four time intervals, we can construct the truth table for the circuit:
Interval 1: $A = 0, B = 0 \Rightarrow Y = 1$
Interval 2: $A = 1, B = 0 \Rightarrow Y = 0$
Interval 3: $A = 0, B = 1 \Rightarrow Y = 0$
Interval 4: $A = 1, B = 1 \Rightarrow Y = 0$

This truth table corresponds to the NOR logic operation, where the output is high only when both inputs are low. The Boolean expression for a NOR gate is $Y = \overline{A + B}$.

According to De Morgan's laws, $\overline{A + B} = \overline{A} \cdot \overline{B}$.

This expression represents taking the complement of $A$ (using a NOT gate), taking the complement of $B$ (using a NOT gate), and then feeding both into an AND gate. Therefore, the correct circuit configuration is input $A$ fed to a NOT gate, input $B$ fed to a NOT gate, and their outputs fed into an AND gate.

Answer: Input $A$ is fed to a NOT gate, input $B$ is fed to a NOT gate, and their outputs are fed into an AND gate.

105425.subject: Physics
105425.text: A screw gauge has a pitch of $1\text{ mm}$ and $100$ divisions on its circular scale. When its jaws are fully closed, the zero of the circular scale is $4$ divisions above the reference line. While measuring the diameter of a wire, the main scale reading is $2\text{ mm}$ and the circular scale reading is $45$ divisions. The true diameter of the wire is:
105425.sol:
Least count (LC) of the screw gauge is:
$\text{LC} = \dfrac{\text{Pitch}}{\text{Number of circular scale divisions}}$
$\text{LC} = \dfrac{1\text{ mm}}{100} = 0.01\text{ mm}$

Since the zero of the circular scale is above the reference line when the jaws are closed, the screw gauge has a negative zero error.
$\text{Zero error} = -4 \times 0.01\text{ mm} = -0.04\text{ mm}$

The observed reading for the wire's diameter is:
$\text{Observed Reading} = \text{MSR} + (\text{CSR} \times \text{LC})$
$\text{Observed Reading} = 2\text{ mm} + (45 \times 0.01\text{ mm}) = 2.45\text{ mm}$

The true reading is obtained by subtracting the zero error from the observed reading:
$\text{True Reading} = \text{Observed Reading} - \text{Zero error}$
$\text{True Reading} = 2.45\text{ mm} - (-0.04\text{ mm}) = 2.49\text{ mm}$

Answer: $2.49\text{ mm}$

108639.subject: Chemistry
108639.text:
Consider the synthesis of ammonia by the Haber process:
$\text{N}_2\text{(g)} + 3\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3\text{(g)}$
At $300$ K, the standard internal energy change ($\Delta U^{\ominus}$) for the reaction is $-87.2$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ and the standard entropy change ($\Delta S^{\ominus}$) is $-198$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$.
Identify the correct option with the standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^{\ominus}$) and the spontaneity of the reaction at $300$ K.
(Given: $R = 8.3$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)
108639.sol:
The change in the number of moles of gaseous species is:

$\Delta n_g = n_p - n_r = 2 - (1 + 3) = -2$

The standard enthalpy change $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ is given by:

$\Delta H^{\ominus} = \Delta U^{\ominus} + \Delta n_g R T$

Substituting the given values (converting $R$ to kJ K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$):

$\Delta H^{\ominus} = -87.2 + (-2) \times (8.3 \times 10^{-3}) \times 300$

$\Delta H^{\ominus} = -87.2 - 4.98 = -92.18 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

The standard Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ is:

$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T \Delta S^{\ominus}$

$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -92.18 - 300 \times (-198 \times 10^{-3})$

$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -92.18 + 59.4 = -32.78 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Since $\Delta G^{\ominus} < 0$, the reaction is spontaneous.

Using $\Delta U^{\ominus}$ directly in place of $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ leads to the incorrect value of $-27.80 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $-32.78$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, spontaneous

111906.subject: Chemistry
111906.text:
Consider the following statements regarding hyperconjugation:

(I) It is a permanent electronic effect.
(II) It involves the delocalization of $\sigma$ electrons.
(III) It is also known as no-bond resonance.
(IV) In carbocations, it involves the overlap of a C-H $\sigma$ bond with an empty p-orbital.

How many of the above statements are correct?
111906.sol:
Statement (I) is correct: Hyperconjugation is a permanent effect, unlike the electromeric effect which is temporary.

Statement (II) is correct: It involves the delocalization of $\sigma$ electrons of a C-H bond of an alkyl group directly attached to an atom of an unsaturated system or to an atom with an unshared p-orbital.

Statement (III) is correct: Since there is no bond between the alpha-carbon and the hydrogen atom in some of the contributing resonance structures, it is also known as no-bond resonance.

Statement (IV) is correct: In carbocations (e.g., ethyl cation), the empty p-orbital of the positively charged carbon overlaps with the $\sigma$ electrons of the adjacent C-H bond.

Therefore, all four statements are correct.

Answer: All four

112644.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Transformation of but-1-ene to butanal can be achieved using $\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6$ followed by $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2/\mathrm{OH}^-$ and subsequently reacting the product with Pyridinium Chlorochromate (PCC).

Reason (R): Hydroboration-oxidation of but-1-ene yields bu\tan^{-1}-ol via anti-Markovnikov addition of water, and primary alcohols are selectively oxidized to aldehydes by PCC.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
112644.sol:
The Assertion is true: the sequence of hydroboration-oxidation ($\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6$ followed by $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2/\mathrm{OH}^-$) converts a terminal alkene (but-1-ene) to a primary alcohol (bu\tan^{-1}-ol). Subsequent oxidation with a mild oxidizing agent like PCC converts the primary alcohol to an aldehyde (butanal) without over-oxidizing it to a carboxylic acid.

The Reason is also true and correctly explains the Assertion: the regioselectivity of hydroboration-oxidation follows anti-Markovnikov addition, placing the hydroxyl group on the less substituted carbon to form bu\tan^{-1}-ol, which is essential for forming the aldehyde upon oxidation with PCC.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
